parsed.title: Simulation and Synthesized Data in Training and Evaluating Driving Policies
outline: Introduction to End-to-End Neural Network Methods
Role of CARLA Simulator in Autonomous Driving Research
parsed.markdown:
End-to-end neural network approaches for autonomous driving utilize convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to map sensory inputs directly to driving commands, exemplified by CNNs learning the entire processing pipeline to steer vehicles [1]. Early systems like ALVINN demonstrated that neural networks trained end-to-end could steer cars on public roads, though with limited reliability compared to modular pipelines [1]. More recent architectures such as ChauffeurNet employ RNNs with mid-level inputs to output driving trajectories, enhancing control capabilities [2].

The CARLA simulator is widely adopted for autonomous driving research, offering open-source urban environments with diverse assets including buildings, vehicles, and pedestrians [3]. It supports flexible sensor configurations and multiple sensing modalities, enabling comprehensive training and validation of driving policies [3]. CARLA facilitates controlled scenario evaluation and closed-loop simulation testing, which are critical for assessing autonomous systems before real-world deployment [3, 2].

Mid-level representations are pivotal in autonomous driving models, allowing training on both real and simulated data and supporting closed-loop simulation validation [2]. These representations sample dynamic objects and agent poses over time, improving data generation from simulations or sensors [2]. Despite these advances, pure imitation learning remains insufficient even with large datasets and mid-level inputs, as models can still fail in complex scenarios [2].

The foundation of autonomous driving models includes extensive data collection efforts, such as the DARPA Autonomous Vehicle (DAVE) project, which trained on hours of human driving data with video and steering commands [1]. This historical groundwork informs current approaches and highlights the importance of diverse training data covering various road types and conditions [1].

However, significant challenges remain. Early end-to-end neural networks, while promising, lack the reliability of modular pipelines and cannot yet fully replace them [1]. Additionally, error accumulation and distribution shift during closed-loop operation present ongoing obstacles to robustness [2]. These gaps underscore the need for further research into hybrid methods and improved learning strategies to enhance autonomous driving performance and safety.
